subject: Computer Networking
title: HTTP/3: The Future of the Web
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: HTTP/3: The Future of the Web.

hook.text: HTTP/1 was simple. HTTP/2 added multiplexing. HTTP/3 throws away TCP entirely and starts fresh with QUIC.

buildup.text: HTTP/3 keeps the same semantics — GET, POST, headers, status codes — but the transport layer is completely new.

discovery.text: Because QUIC handles encryption natively, HTTP/3 connections set up faster than HTTP/2 over TLS.

twist.text: HTTP/3 handles network switches gracefully. Move from Wi-Fi to cellular? The connection survives seamlessly.

climax.text: Google, Cloudflare, and Facebook already serve traffic over HTTP/3. Adoption is accelerating rapidly.

punchline.text: HTTP/3 is HTTP rebuilt on a faster foundation.

quiz.question: What transport protocol does HTTP/3 use instead of TCP?
options: A new version of TCP called TCP/2

details.summary: HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC as its transport layer, eliminating TCP's head-of-line blocking and reducing connection setup time. QUIC builds encryption, multiplexing, and reliability directly into the transport layer over UDP, enabling faster page loads especially on unreliable mobile networks.
details.whyItMatters: HTTP/3 solves the last major performance bottleneck of web communication. By moving to QUIC over UDP, it delivers faster connections and better resilience on mobile and lossy networks.
takeaways: HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP instead of TCP for transport
Zero-RTT connection resumption enables instant reconnections
Per-stream error recovery eliminates head-of-line blocking

faq.question: How is HTTP/3 faster than HTTP/2?
faq.answer: HTTP/2 over TCP suffers head-of-line blocking when a single packet is lost, stalling all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC where each stream is independent, so one lost packet only affects its own stream. QUIC also combines the TLS handshake with connection setup, saving a round trip.

faq.question: Is HTTP/3 widely supported?
faq.answer: All major browsers and many CDNs support HTTP/3. Google, Cloudflare, and Facebook already serve significant traffic over HTTP/3. Adoption is growing rapidly. Server software like Nginx and Caddy support it natively, and cloud load balancers are adding HTTP/3 termination.
